what_it_does: Google's data centers run thousands of different data-processing jobs and must decide for each one whether to store its temporary files on fast-but-expensive solid-state drives (SSDs) or cheaper-but-slower spinning hard disk drives (HDDs). Machine-learning models could make much better decisions than simple rules, but putting one model inside the storage system breaks as soon as any workload changes. This paper's 'Bring-Your-Own-Model' approach lets each workload train its own small ML model at the application layer and pass a simple ranking hint down to the storage layer, which combines hints from all workloads using a self-adjusting admission rule — achieving up to 3.47x more cost savings than the current production baseline.
method_in_detail:
The idea. A monolithic model in the storage layer must know about every workload's access patterns to make good decisions — but workloads change constantly, storage systems update slowly, and a single failing model takes down everything. The fix: each application trains its own lightweight model that knows only its own workload, and passes a simple 'importance score' downward. The storage layer never needs to understand any particular application.

How it works. Offline, each workload (or cluster of similar workloads) trains a gradient-boosted decision tree — a fast, interpretable model similar to a flow chart — on historical job metadata: how much data the job reads and writes, how long it lives, what time of day it runs, which pipeline it belongs to. The model predicts an 'importance category' for each new job (0 = would cost more to put on SSD than it saves; 1 through N = ranked by how dense the job's I/O is relative to its storage footprint).

The key design choice. The importance category is designed to be independent of the current SSD fill level — it ranks how inherently valuable a job is, not whether there is room. A separate algorithm at the storage layer — called Adaptive Category Selection (ACS) — handles the dynamic part. ACS watches a running metric called 'spillover TCIO' (the fraction of jobs that were supposed to go on SSD but got pushed to HDD because SSD was full). If spillover is rising, ACS raises its admission cutoff, accepting only the highest-importance jobs; if SSDs have headroom, it lowers the cutoff to let in lower-priority jobs too. The threshold moves one step at a time to avoid oscillation, and only changes at fixed intervals.

The catch. A perfectly accurate model does not guarantee perfectly optimal placement — the category design and the adaptive algorithm interact, and improvements beyond moderate model accuracy yield diminishing returns.

The result. In a live test deployment at Google with 320 servers and 1,024 shuffle jobs, Adaptive Ranking saves 4.38x more storage total cost of ownership (TCO) than the simple rule-based baseline at 1% SSD quota, and 1.77x at 20% quota. Across 10 large production clusters in simulation, the system achieves up to 3.47x TCO savings over the state-of-the-art baseline, with inference latency of about 4 ms per job.
